replying_to: Replying to A Note on Quantifying the Influence of Energy Regularization for Imbalanced Classification
display_title: Official Review of Paper3548 by Reviewer 4hgM

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper examines the problem of constructing a classifier that generalizes well to out-of-distribution examples. The proposed method adds a regularizer to a trained model and then finetunes using this regularized objective. The regularizer is the sum over the energy values (i.e. the normalizing constant of the softmax outputs of a classifier) of each training point, where each training energy value is weighted by its estimated influence on the prediction error on the validation set. Points with positive correlation (i.e. those for which upweighting the energy function would have a positive impact on validation error) are upweighted in the regularizer, and those with negative correlation are downweighted in the regularizer.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The proposed method makes sense at a high level -- we've found something that correlates well with the validation objective, and so we should tell the model to pay more attention to that thing. But this raises a few questions: why not just use the validation objective itself as a "regularizer" (so, more training data)? Is there a sense in which the energy function is an optimal (or even good) function to use here? We could propose *any* function of the training data $x_{tr}$ and do the same thing. So why are we using energy functions?

The paper computes influence functions for deep learning methods as is done in Koh and Liang (2017). Since the publication of that paper, there have been some issues brought up with their method that I think should be addressed in the current paper. (1) influence functions assume the loss is convex, which is definitely violated here (influence functions are derived by an expansion around a unique local minimum of a function). It is not clear what the correct generalization of an "influence function" is under non-convexity. Second, the stochastic matrix inverse method used by Koh and Liang (2017) can be very inaccurate (side note, the authors reference Cook & Weisberg (1982) in the appendix for this method, but the correct reference is Agarwal et al. (2017)). See Basu et al. (2021) and Stephenson et al. (2020) for examples of this method failing. (3) Basu et al. (2021) show that influence functions can be inaccurate specifically in deep learning. Put together, I think there need to be experiments showing why we should trust the use of influence functions as they are used in the current paper.

In the experiments, the proposed method does seem to perform better than competing methods. But the gains look extremely small. Standard deviations need to be reported so we can understand whether these gains are significant. Also, even if they gains are statistically significant, I'm not sure that they are substantial enough to warrant using an entirely new method (e.g. all of the gains are less than 1% in terms of test accuracy, and many are less than 0.1%). I think more compelling experiments are needed. In particular, the authors might try to understand *when* their method provides gains and demonstrate its performance in those situations. This would have the dual benefit of both showing strong results and helping the community understand what regularization by energy is really doing.

Overall, it would be good to have some more motivation for the use of energy as a regularizer. The authors write "Remark 1 tells us that optimizing the classifier would, in fact, lead to an unstable shift of the energy value. Thus, we argue that the energy value needs to be explicitly regularized." This seems like a critical part of the paper that tells us why we should regularize by energy. I think this part of the paper should be expanded a lot. First, I don't see why Remark 1 implies that the energy will be "unstable" during optimization (what is definition of unstable?). Second, and more importantly, why does this instability imply that we need to regularize by the energy. For example, what does instability in the energy have to do with out-of-distribution generalization?

More scattered comments:
- The introduction goes back and forth on talking about class imbalance and distribution shift. Which is the focus of the paper?
- The paper never really explains what an influence function is. E.g. why are we using it to weight the regularizer? I think it's easy for someone who's used influence functions to answer this question, but the paper shouldn't leave readers guessing.
- "Since the energy value defined in Eq. 2 reflects the predicted $p(x)$". I didn't follow what $p(x)$ has to do with prediction up to this point -- it seems like we're predicting $y$ and not $p(x)$.
- Is proposition 1 supposed to hold for all $y$? If so, state it.
- In the definition of $\hat\theta_{\epsilon, (x_{tr}, y_{tr})}$, $y_{tr}$ is not used.
- The minus sign in front of the energy regularization term isn't consistent throughout (e.g. compare Eq. (10) and (11) and the definition of $\hat\theta_{\epsilon, (x_{tr}, y_{tr})}$).


**References**
- N. Agarwal, B. Bullins, and E. Hazan. Second order stochastic optimization in linear time. JMLR. 2017.
- S. Basu, P. Pope, and S. Feizi. Influence Functions in Deep Learning Are Fragile. ICLR. 2021.
- W. T. Stephenson, M. Udell and T. Broderick. Approximate Cross-Validation with Low-Rank Data in High Dimensions. NeurIPS. 2020.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The writing is fine at a high-level, but can be somewhat unclear when it comes to more technical points (e.g. the discussion of why we should regularize by energy functions).
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I think the paper needs more motivation for regularizing by the energy, justification that influence functions are working well here, and compelling experiments.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper shows that the energy value has an influence on the classifier when test data and training data have different class priors. An energy regularization term is then proposed to finetune a model. Empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
+ The authors show that during the training process, the energy fluctuates regarding the output of the model as the loss decreases. In general, well-classified samples would generally have lower energy.
+ The authors show that even with two classifiers with identical predictions, the energy could be different. 

Weakness:
+ The technical insight may not be enough. From my perspective, the energy seems can be approximated with the cross-entropy loss.  An example with small energy should also have small losses. Then optimizing the classifier of course leads to an unstable shift of the loss value.
+The hyper-parameter has to be carefully selected. In general, well-classified samples would generally have lower energy. By empirical risk minimization, the energy is expected to decrease. However, because of the strong fitting ability of DNN models, increasing the energy value might can prevent overfitting. The problem is that the weight of energy regularization has to be chosen carefully to make the regularization not harmful. This hyper-parameter can be very different for different datasets. 
+More baselines for preventing overfitting or learning with class-imbalance data should be compared.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper generally is well written. The method is simple and easy to reproduce.
content.summary_of_the_review: My largest concern is that the technical insight may not be that strong and the experiments are insufficient.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes to regularize the energy to improve model predictions when the training data has few samples from some classes. The idea seems to be that classifiers can help detect OOD samples due to the "energy" and regularizing the influence of energy should help improve the classifier learn better on the classes with few samples.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper points out an interesting way to combat label imbalance which is quite a different way from how imbalance has been handled in the literature.

Weaknesses:

1. The paper uses influence functions that have been shown to be fragile for neural networks (https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.14651). Can the authors explain why they believe their given influence-based regularization is expected to work while they do not in other cases?
2. The experiments do not lend sufficient support to the method. Reporting standard deviations over multiple runs would be a start because in most of the columns in Table 1, the improvement that energy regularization provides over LDAM-DRW is under 1%. The story is similar for table 2.
3. The paper's writing made it hard for me to understand why and where the improvements are coming from. See next section.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper was hard for me to read due to the motivation being vague and few sentences either unclear or unjustified:

1. Why is this true? : " well-classified samples would generally have lower energy ". Accuracy does not seem to have anything to do with energy.
2. The word imbalance is used to denote covariate shift (where $p(X)$ changes) but mainly talks about long-tail classification. This is unclear because covariate shift is a more general setting which may or may not have class imbalance.
3. Section 3.4 requires further text supporting the claim. Energy-regularization appearing as weighting is probably fine but the way the regularization affects the margin seems to depend on the value of $\beta$. If $\beta > 1$,  then a negative gradient step will increase margin.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper studies an interesting way to tackle class imbalance but the writing needs improvement and the value of the proposed method is unclear.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to study the "energy function" of a classifier defined as the log_sum_exp of the logits. It argues that the energy values are indicative of model's performance when trained on imbalanced datasets. It then proposes an influence function based regularization of the energy values which improves over the baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
1. Addressing the distribution shift problem is an interesting and important problem. 
2. The proposed method which regularizes the energy values based on each examples influence is reasonable.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
1. Motivation and presentation. First of all, I don't feel like the energy function $E(x)$ or the marginal distribution of data $p(x)$ is justified. While it is true that given the soft max parameterization of a classifier, one can indeed derive a joint distribution $p(x, y)$ which gives rise to both the conditional $p(y|x)$ and $p(x)$, there is no guarantee that training the conditional $p(y|x)$ alone learns anything about the joint $p(x, y)$, or $p(x)$. As a matter of fact, one needs to significantly modify the training procedure to include a negative sampling phase of x (eg va MCMC or contrastive divergence) in order to make any claims about the marginal $p(x)$. That being said, $E(x)$ is still potentially a useful quantity to look at or regularize, but it will require a different motivation and presentation. 

2. Methodology. The influence function is indeed an interesting and powerful tool to address the class imbalance issue, however, I do not see an organic connection between the influence function and the energy function. One can argue that the proposed reweighting technique can be directly applied to each training examples loss. What makes the energy especially suited or useful in this case?

3. Experiments. The comparison with baselines is not fair. The proposed method has access to a validation set which is also assumed to be balanced. This makes it unfair to compare to both the ERM baseline and others that do not have the same input.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall I think this work needs significant improvements on several aspects as mentioned before, I believe it's not yet ready for publishing.
